atoms.text: Over time, some Celtic hillforts grew larger and developed into oppida — a new style of town.
atoms.sound: Over time, some Celtic hill-forts grew larger and developed into oppida — a new style of town.

atoms.text: Key advancements included gravel streets in a grid pattern, more stone buildings and wells for water within the settlement walls.
Many oppida also became centres for activities like metalwork and trading. By producing valuables, they were able to get foreign goods from Roman traders.

feedback.finish: The failed invasion still introduced some Britons to new Roman products, such as olive oil and wine. Trading for these luxuries became very popular.

atoms.b: Calleva Atrebatum was one of the oppida that became most ((++similar different)) to Roman towns. This was because the tribe’s king, Commius, was originally from a part of the empire called Gaul and was already used to the Roman ((++lifestyle liberties)).
atoms.sound: Callayva Atrabartum was one of the opp-ida that became most similar to Roman towns. This was because the tribe’s king, Commius, was originally from a part of the empire called Gaul and was already used to the Roman lifestyle.

atoms.b: Commius built a mint to make coins in the ((++Roman Gallic)) style — with his name on them. Calleva Atrebatum also became a centre for ((++gold grass)) refinement, making valuable jewellery alongside these coins.
atoms.sound: Commius built a mint to make coins in the Roman style — with his name on them. Callayva Atrabartum also became a centre for gold refinement, making valuable jewellery alongside these coins.

atoms.b: Commius also had a good relationship with Roman ((++merchants mermaids)). Historians have found evidence that Calleva Atrebatum had olive oil, wine and a type of Roman fish sauce called garum — all of which could only have come from ((++trade treasure))!
